Limitations_or_Caveats: The 2023 field study visited 49 households across the overall study in Cachar, Hailakandi and Sribhumi, but the reviewed text does not provide a village-by-beverage or household-by-community allocation. The Haria subsection's detailed Dabai recipe cites a 2014 Haria study from lateritic West Bengal; confirm which details derive from original southern Assam interviews before treating them as Assam-specific. Ndhui gei remains unidentified; cultural/medicinal statements are not clinical evidence.

Author_or_Organisation: Atungbou, N.
Title: Food practice for physical and spiritual well-being of the Zeme, the tribe in Northeast India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed original article, Journal of Ethnic Foods 7, article 41

Author_or_Organisation: Longkumer, A.

Author_or_Organisation: Directorate of Information & Public Relations, Government of Mizoram
Title: The Origin of the Chapchar Kut

Author_or_Organisation: Sonowal, R.
Title: Traditional Rice Beer Fermentation Technology of the Sonowal Kachari Tribe of Assam, India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Participatory ethnographic and technical article, Antrocom Online Journal of Anthropology 19(1), 605–613
Geographic_Scope: Jokai area, Dibrugarh district, Assam

Claims_Supported: Describes Rohi production, Mod pitha/Saul pitha starter, glutinous rice, equipment and process, 4–5-day fermentation (longer in winter), and festival/ritual/social contexts.

Author_or_Organisation: Bhattacharya, B.; Chandra Deka, D.
Title: Preparation, physicochemical analysis and antioxidant properties of Rohi and Sepa: traditional rice beers of the Sonowal Kacharis, Assam
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed article, Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge 25(9), 914–921
Geographic_Scope: Sonowal Kachari community in Assam; precise sampling locality not stated in repository abstract
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Sonowal Kachari Rohi and Sepa
Claims_Supported: Identifies Rohi and Sepa as traditional rice-based fermented alcoholic beverages using Mod pitha starter; reports cultural/social importance and evaluates physicochemical parameters and antioxidant properties.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Only the repository abstract was accessible in this review; Sepa-specific recipe, sampling village, and distinction from Rohi need full-text extraction. Antioxidant assay findings do not establish clinical health benefits.

Author_or_Organisation: Das, R.; Medhi, M. C.; Tamang, B.
Title: Microbial diversity and its links to retinol pathways and aroma compounds in ethnic fermented rice beverages of Assam
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed research article, AMB Express 16, article 91
Geographic_Scope: Pukia, Dhemaji district (Black Rohi Modh and Rohi Modh); Kaljar, Baksa district (Jou Bidwi); Jamuuri Panchali, Dhemaji district (Sai Mod)
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Black Rohi Modh; Rohi Modh; Jou Bidwi; Sai Mod

The article's broad Kachari label and citation to Sonowal (2023) do not establish that Rohi Modh is a distinct community-named tradition from Sonowal Kachari Rohi. Black Rohi Modh is recorded provisionally as a substrate-associated variant pending local terminology confirmation. Antioxidant assays and predicted pathways do not establish clinical benefits.

Author_or_Organisation: Assam Tourism Development Corporation / Assam Tourism
Title: Culinary Treasures of Assam: A Food Lover's Dream — Rice Beer section

Geographic_Scope: Assam; community-specific districts and villages are not provided in this section

Treat as a discovery lead only and corroborate with community-specific and scholarly sources before asserting canonical records.

Author_or_Organisation: Talukdar, S.; Jyethi, D. S.; Sarma, B.; et al.
Title: Cultural ecology and conservation of traditional beverage practices among selected communities of Assam, Northeast India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed original research article, Discover Food 6, article 376

Some statements are broad or not consistently community-specific; treat cultural claims as study findings rather than universal rules. It does not mention Hajang Jatha Kasa/Ruhi, Rabha Matha Mod/Roshi Mod or Tai-Ahom Luk-Lau, so it does not resolve those name leads. Medicinal or health-related claims require independent evidence.

Author_or_Organisation: Ministry of Women and Child Development, Government of India
Title: An Exploratory Study on Indigenous Food of North-East India — Kesa mod/Jonga mod entry

Limitations_or_Caveats: The accessible excerpt does not identify an exact village and uses Ruhi as an extraction tool in a Rabha Kesa/Jonga mod preparation. It does not establish that Ruhi is a Hajang beverage. Other food-processing literature uses Ruhi for a different rice-based alcoholic beverage in Nagaland/eastern hill regions; these usages must not be conflated.

Author_or_Organisation: Bhattacharya, B.; Deka, D. C.

Limitations_or_Caveats: Full text is hosted on ResearchGate; exact villages and community-preferred product names are not confirmed in the accessible abstract. Do not infer that these products are synonyms for Janga, Jonga-mod, Matha Mod or Roshi Mod.

Publication_or_Source_Type: Research article; Asian Journal of Chemistry 36(1), 201–205

Authors' comparisons to drinking-water metal limits do not establish that alcohol is safe overall.

Claims_Supported: Describes boiled rice inoculated with yeast grown on rice and nosan leaves; liquid is collected as rice ferments and may be transferred to fresh boiled rice several times; reports ethanol range of 12–14% v/v.

Author_or_Organisation: Sarma, Rabindranath
Title: Rice Beer and tribes of Assam

Do not equate Garo Su, Deuri Sujhen and other similarly sounding terms. It cites older secondary works and contains historical claims that should not be treated as current prevalence.

Author_or_Organisation: Loying, P.; et al. (full author list to verify from article metadata)

Limitations_or_Caveats: Secondary review, not a village-level survey. Exact Assam village, current prevalence, and relationship between Chu, Su and Chubitchi are unresolved. Do not transfer Meghalaya Chubitchi's recipe to Assam Chu without evidence.

Author_or_Organisation: Deka, D.; Sarma, G. C.

Claims_Supported: Primary article reports ten starter-cake plant species and names them in Table 1. Explicitly describes finished rice beer as choko or jonga-mod in its Goalpara Rabha context; supports local alternate naming without proving universal equivalence across other localities or subgroups.
Limitations_or_Caveats: The accessible full text does not identify a village list or confirm whether Kecha-mod, West Bengal Chokot/Chokoth, Matha Mod or Roshi Mod are synonyms, variants or distinct products. Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Tai-Ahom Xaj-pani/Xaj; Xajor pitha; rohi
Claims_Supported: Reports an in-person xaj-making and tasting visit in Goahai Gaon; describes household-specific starter preparation, bora rice, earthen koloh, 3–5 day fermentation, filtering, serving customs and collection of rohi.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Journalistic ethnographic feature, not a systematic survey; ingredient list/proportions are one household account and the author notes some proportions were not disclosed. Reported medicinal use of rohi is a household belief, not clinical evidence; the article's historical claims require independent corroboration.

Author_or_Organisation: Borah, D.; Gogoi, T.; Sarma, J.; Borah, P. J.; Gohain, B.; Mili, C.; Upadhyaya, A.; Basumatary, J.; Neog, K.; Wangpan, T.; Tangjang, S.

Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Traditional beverage and starter-culture plant knowledge; Xaj/Haj, Jou, Hor, Apong including Po:ro apong
Claims_Supported: Reports participatory field investigations with 202 respondents, documenting 129 plant species associated with traditional alcoholic beverage preparation across the four named communities. The Po:ro-specific methods section describes ash-assisted fermentation and Ta:suk water extraction/filtration. A separate section reports distillation in three communities (not Ahom) and describes a generic distillation apparatus/process.
Limitations_or_Caveats: The paper's summary associations (Ahom Haaj/Laupani, Bodo Jou/Bishi, Karbi Hor/Hor-alank, Mising Poro apong/Sai mod) are study-wide and are not allocated to each district. Reviewed main text does not name all 32 villages or map community/beverage to each district. Do not infer that every community or beverage occurs in every study district. Po:ro apong ash/extraction account is source-specific; separate generic distillation section is not explicitly identified as a Po:ro stage.

Author_or_Organisation: Bhattacharya, S.; Deka, D. C.; et al. (verify full author metadata)

Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Secondary district leads: Adivasi/Haria associated with Morigaon, Golaghat, Sonitpur, Nagaon, Jorhat and Bongaigaon; Bodo beverages associated with Kokrajhar, Chirang, Baksa and Udalguri; Mech Kachari terms Haaz, Photika, Jau and districts including Udalguri, Kokrajhar and Goalpara
Claims_Supported: A secondary review table lists these community/district associations and terms; useful for discovery and follow-up searches where the archive lacks a place row.

Do not assign Haria, Jou variants or Mech Kachari names to individual villages without primary/local evidence; do not assume Haaz, Photika and Jau are synonyms.

Author_or_Organisation: Dutta, Palash

Geographic_Scope: Deori community in Assam; broad community-level account, no named village for the beverage passage
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Jau/Jumai (fermented rice beer); Photika (distilled liquor prepared from Jau/Jumai)
Claims_Supported: Describes Jau/Jumai as a Deori rice beer and Photika as a distilled liquor made from it; discusses hospitality, social functions and offerings in the Deori context.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Secondary socio-cultural account with limited methodological detail and no named production village. It is useful as a cross-check because a later review also lists Jau and Photika under Mech Kachari; that discrepancy requires tracing the review citations and does not itself prove exclusive ownership or disprove use by another community.

Author_or_Organisation: Senapati, S. S.; Gurumayum, S.

Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Traditional beverage starter cultures and plant ingredients; comparative source for checking later review citations
Claims_Supported: Reviews starter-cake preparation, fermentation practices and plant ingredients across eight named communities; useful as a separate literature trail for traditional beverage methods and plant-use claims.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Secondary review rather than village-level field survey. Its abstract does not list Mech Kachari among the eight communities discussed, so it does not independently substantiate the Mech Kachari Haaz/Photika/Jau table in Bhattacharya and Deka (2023). Do not use broad plant claims as village-specific evidence or clinical proof of medicinal effects.

Author_or_Organisation: Bhuyan, B.; Baishya, K.

Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Bodo Jou bishi; Karbi Horlang; Ahom Haj/Koloh pani; Rabha Jonga/Kecha mod; Mising Apong; Deori Sujen; Sonowal Kachari Rohi and related starter-plant traditions
Claims_Supported: Synthesizes ethnomedicinal plants and traditional rice-beer/starter information across seven named communities; secondary cross-check for beverage terminology and selected localities
Limitations_or_Caveats: Review article, not a new village census. Named places may refer to informants, cited studies or study contexts; do not infer current prevalence, universal recipes, clinical medicinal efficacy, or synonymy between similarly named beverages. Confirm locality attribution against the article text and underlying sources.

Author_or_Organisation: Deka, A. K.; Basumatary, S.; Deka, D. C.

Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Bodo Jou/Joubidwi, stored Joufinai, Kanthal-Jougwran (jackfruit), Kola-Jougwran (banana), Kamrenga-bidwi (starfruit), Amlai-bidwi (gooseberry), Amao starter
Claims_Supported: Reports interviews with 50 people and detailed methods for stored rice-based and fruit-based Bodo beverages, including ingredients, fermentation/storage periods, local vessel names and a traditional distillation setup

Author_or_Organisation: Kumari, S.; Ama, T.; Jyoti Koch, P.; Debbarma, R.

Publication_or_Source_Type: Original research article; Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge 24(7):615–626

Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Opo starter; Nyishi rice-wine varieties named Tisar, Kecha and Adak
Claims_Supported: Characterizes physicochemical and biochemical properties of traditional Nyishi rice-wine varieties; identifies Opo as the traditional starter culture and reports sample-specific differences among Tisar, Kecha and Adak.

The abstract does not identify sampling villages or give enough evidence to decide whether Tisar, Kecha and Adak are beverage names, variety labels, or locality-specific forms.

Author_or_Organisation: Hoikhokim; Laldinthar, R.; Haokip, H.; Lhungdim, N.
Title: An Indigenous Fermented Rice beverage (Anthom) and its Ethnomedicinal and Cultural Uses by the Thadou-Kuki tribes in Manipur, India

Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Anthom; sticky/glutinous rice, black or white varieties; starter called Chol; liquid fraction called aning
Claims_Supported: Documents Anthom as a fermented rice beverage and describes a source-specific process using cooked sticky rice, Chol starter, a covered vessel and fermentation for 3–7 days; the liquid fraction is called aning.
Limitations_or_Caveats: The paper reports ethnomedicinal uses as traditional claims, not clinical evidence. Village-level sampling and prevalence are not established in the accessible record; recipe and social-use descriptions should not be generalized to all Thadou-Kuki households.

Author_or_Organisation: Gogoi, P.; Konwar, S.; Das, S.; Das, D.; Doimari, R.; Sonar, T.; Doley, S.

Claims_Supported: Documents Mising Po:ro Apong and Noggin Apong, starter-cake preparation and household methods within a 10-village Jorhat field study with 50 informants; article provides a named village list and process descriptions, but does not map each beverage subtype to each village.
Limitations_or_Caveats: The article states voucher specimens were not collected or deposited, so no herbarium voucher verification is available. Village list is study scope, not evidence that both beverage forms are prepared in every village. Consent wording is internally uneven: the methods say prior consent 'should be taken' but later claim prior informed consent was obtained; interpret ethical assurance cautiously rather than inferring misconduct. Reported medicinal/nutritional benefits are not clinical evidence. Some process wording may need linguistic clarification; compare with primary sources and community-preferred terminology.

The paper’s claims that products are prepared by all tribes should not be treated as a verified universal distribution. Traditional medicinal claims are not clinical evidence.

Author_or_Organisation: Borah, Porismita

Author_or_Organisation: Das, Santanu; Özkurt, Ezgi; Joishy, Tulsi Kumari; Mukherjee, Ashis K.; Hildebrand, Falk; Khan, Mojibur R.

Claims_Supported: Reports a seven-village survey used to screen potential volunteers and a final analysis cohort of 166 (142 Mising Apong consumers and 24 monk controls); methods identify participants from Telam, Dhemaji and Majuli districts. It does not name the seven villages in the accessible text or assign each beverage to individual villages. Health associations are observational and cannot establish causation or safety; alcohol consumption is not a health recommendation.

The PMC full text labels its supplementary DOCX as available to authorized users; the file could not be retrieved through the accessible route in this review, so village names and sample-to-village mapping remain unverified. Laboratory analysis of selected samples is not a representative survey of all production. Health-related interpretation is exploratory and not proof of benefit or safety.

Author_or_Organisation: Mili, Chiranjib; Lagachu, Manab Jyoti; Basumatary, Jwngma; Tayung, Kumananda

Full text was not accessible in this review; claims should be cross-checked against cited primary studies. Do not treat flavour/chemical discussion as evidence of clinical benefit or safety.

Author_or_Organisation: Pegu, Rajeswar; Gogoi, Jitu; Tamuli, Ajit K.; Teron, Robindra

Claims_Supported: Documents traditional knowledge using discussions, semi-structured interviews and personal observations. Describes Po:ro extraction through a leaf-lined conical bamboo Ta:suk with straw at the base, adding water to draw off the liquid; Nogin is separately extracted by stirring fermented rice with water and sieving.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Fieldwork is dated 2010 and 2012 and should be treated as historical, source-specific documentation. Reported community beliefs about health effects are not clinical evidence. Author_or_Organisation: Talukdar, Simi; Jyethi, Darpa Saurav; Sarma, Barasa; Talukdar, Homen
Title: Cultural ecology and conservation of traditional beverage practices among selected communities of Assam, Northeast India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed open-access research article; Discover Food 6:376
Geographic_Scope: Fieldwork in Kokrajhar and Baksa (Bodo), Goalpara and Kamrup (Rabha), and Tinsukia and Dibrugarh (Ahom), Assam; fieldwork reported for February 2023–2024

Limitations_or_Caveats: Study-site districts are not a production census and do not establish village-level beverage attribution. Table 1 attributes plants to communities but has no beverage-specific column. Audit of archived transcription: 41 rows and 41 distinct scientific-name strings; community labels occur on 35 Ahom, 20 Bodo and 16 Rabha rows; only 8 rows are labelled for all three communities although the narrative says 24/41. Narrative life-form counts sum to 47 against 41 species; table-row labels count 13 herbs, 10 shrubs, 9 trees, 4 climbers, 3 ferns, 1 small tree and 1 woody climber. Methods describe FL as percentage x100 but reported values are mostly around 1–4; scale/formula needs clarification. Preserve source values; do not silently correct. Table 1 prints ST/EES/2024/015 for two taxa; verify against herbarium records. Community-reported medicinal uses are not clinical evidence, and conservation effects are not established causally by the qualitative design. See research/assam/cross-community-2026-source-quality-audit.md and research/assam/src-091-voucher-audit.md.

Author_or_Organisation: Yumnam, H.; Hazarika, P.; Sharma, I.
